Propeller effects

Why you need right rudder on take-off and in the climb: torque, spiral slipstream, P-factor and gyroscopic precession, each with its own arrow. Then lose an engine on a twin and see why one engine is critical and what sets Vmca.

In the climb the angle of attack is high, so the descending blade on the right bites harder than the rising one: that is P-factor. Together with the slipstream it needs steady right rudder. Lower the nose and the P-factor shrinks.

Both propellers turn clockwise from the cockpit, so the descending blade, which gives more thrust at high angle of attack, is on the right of each engine. On the right engine that is farther from the fuselage: a longer arm. Lose the left engine and the right one yaws you harder. The left engine is critical. P-factor is the main reason; accelerated slipstream, spiralling slipstream and torque all point the same way.

In the aircraft
Take-off

Expect the nose to go left as power comes up and right rudder to increase as the speed is low and the slipstream strong. Lead with rudder, keep the centreline, and keep the feet active through the rotation.

Climb and slow flight

High power, high angle of attack, low speed: all the left-turning effects add up. Keep the ball centred with right rudder or rudder trim. A go-around is the classic moment to be caught out.

What sets Vmca

Vmca is determined under the classic certification conditions (CS/FAR 23.149, used for aircraft such as the DA42): critical engine suddenly inoperative with its propeller windmilling (or feathered if auto-feather is fitted), maximum take-off power on the live engine, rearmost CG, take-off flaps, gear up, trimmed for take-off, out of ground effect, and no more than 5° bank toward the live engine. Any of these better, and the real Vmca is lower.

Bank toward the live engine

A few degrees of bank toward the live engine, with the ball about half out toward it, removes the sideslip. Less rudder is needed and the climb performance is best. Wings level with the ball centred means you are slipping.

Losing directional control

Below Vmca the rudder cannot hold the yaw. The fix is to reduce power on the live engine and lower the nose: you lose height, but you get control back. In training this is flown with the power, never by feathering at low height.

Gyroscopic precession

A force on a spinning disc acts 90° later in the direction of rotation. Pitching the nose down yaws left, yawing right pitches the nose down. It matters in taildraggers when the tail comes up, and in aerobatics.

CG and stability

Move the centre of gravity and watch what it does: the tail load, the stall speed, how heavy the controls feel, and how the aircraft answers a gust. Behind the neutral point it stops coming back by itself. Then tune dihedral and fin size and meet the spiral and the Dutch roll.

A big fin and little dihedral: the aircraft is very keen to point into the relative wind, but slow to level the wings. A small bank grows into a steepening, descending spiral. Most light aircraft are slightly spirally unstable, which is why an aircraft left to itself in cloud, with no one flying it on instruments, slowly ends up in a spiral dive.

Load factor is lift divided by weight. In a level turn it is 1/cos(bank): 1.15 g at 30°, 1.41 g at 45°, 2 g at 60°. The stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor, so at 60° bank you stall at about 1.41 × Vs. The curved stall line shows the most load you can pull at each speed: below it, the wing stalls before the structure is overloaded. The manoeuvring speed (VO in CS-23, VA on older types) is where the stall line meets the limit load, here +3.8 g for the normal category: below it, a full control input stalls the wing first. VO falls with the square root of the mass, so a light aircraft must be flown slower in turbulence. Above VNO, a strong gust can exceed the limit load, which is why the yellow arc is for smooth air only.

In the aircraft
Forward CG

More tail down-force means the wing carries more: stall speed and fuel burn go up. Heavy in pitch, and with two up front and nothing behind you may not have enough elevator for the flare.

Aft CG

Light stick forces, easy to over-rotate on take-off and to pull too much g. Stall recovery is slower and a spin may become flat. Never fly behind the aft limit, and remember the CG moves as fuel burns.

Fuel burn and CG

Check the CG at take-off and at landing (zero fuel as a worst case on some types). If the tank is aft of the CG, the CG moves forward as you burn fuel, and the other way round.

Spiral dive in cloud

Spiral instability is slow and quiet: the bank grows, the nose drops, speed and g build. Recovery: power idle, level the wings first, then ease out of the dive.

Trim and stability

A stable aircraft holds the speed it is trimmed for. Out of trim, it keeps pushing back toward that speed. Feeling that push is the stick force the CG controls.

Where the numbers come from

The CG envelope is in the flight manual, the empty mass and arm in your aircraft’s weighing report. Use the mass and balance page in the briefing pack to load your flight.

Aircraft engines

Four engines, taken apart: the diesel piston engine in the DA42, a turboprop, a turbojet and a high-bypass turbofan. Pull them apart, drag any part away, click it to see what it does, what the pressure and temperature are there, what can go wrong, and what you see in the cockpit.

Take it apart
Which engine for which job
In the cockpit
Test yourself
Take it apart
Piston (diesel)
Turboprop
Turbojet
Turbofan
How it works: Turbofan
The big fan at the front pulls in a huge amount of air. Most of it goes around the core (bypass) and gives most of the thrust.
The rest goes into the core: low- and high-pressure compressors squeeze it, and fuel burns continuously in the combustion chamber.
The high-pressure turbine drives the high-pressure compressor through the outer shaft.
The low-pressure turbine drives the fan and the low-pressure compressor through the inner shaft. The two spools turn at different speeds (N1 and N2).

In short: moving a lot of air a little faster is far more efficient and quieter than moving a little air very fast. That is why airliners use turbofans.

TURBOFAN
Fan

The fan is the first stage of the low-pressure (LP) spool: about 16–36 wide, twisted blades of titanium or carbon-fibre composite. It raises the pressure only about 1.4–1.7 times, but it moves an enormous mass of air. In a high-bypass engine it makes around 80 % of the thrust.

The reason is propulsive efficiency. Thrust is mass flow times the change in velocity, but the energy you waste is in the speed of the jet you leave behind. Accelerating a lot of air a little is far more efficient than accelerating a little air a lot. That is the whole idea of the turbofan.

Tip speed is supersonic at take-off; the shock waves are part of the buzz-saw noise you hear in the cabin.
The fan case is wrapped in Kevlar and must contain a released blade (blade-off test in certification).
Birds, ice, hail and loose objects (FOD) hit the fan first.
IN THE COCKPIT
N1 is the fan speed in % of a reference rpm and is the main thrust setting on many engines (others use EPR). Engine vibration is mostly fan vibration.
Which engine for which job

All four make thrust the same way: they push air (or gas) backwards, and the reaction pushes the aircraft forwards. The difference is how much air they move and how fast they throw it. A propeller moves a lot of air slowly, a turbojet a little air very fast. Propulsive efficiency is highest when the jet is only a little faster than the aircraft, which is why each engine has a speed range where it is best.

Engine	Best speed range	Strengths	Weaknesses	Typical aircraft
Piston (avgas or diesel)	up to about 200 kt, below FL200	Cheap, efficient at low power, diesel burns Jet A-1	Heavy for its power, power falls with altitude unless turbocharged	C172, PA-28, DA40, DA42
Turboprop	about 250–350 kt, FL150–FL300	Very efficient on short sectors, good field performance, reliable	Propeller tip speed limits cruise speed; noise and vibration	King Air, PC-12, ATR 72, Dash 8
Turbofan	about Mach 0.7–0.85, FL300–FL410	Efficient and quiet at high subsonic speed, high thrust	Thirsty low and slow, slow to spool up from idle	A320, 737, CJ4, E-Jet
Turbojet	supersonic, or where weight and cost matter more than fuel	Simple, small frontal area, works at very high speed	Loud and very thirsty at low speed	Early jets, missiles, some military
In the cockpit
Starting a turbine engine

Starter on, rotation rising, fuel in at the right speed, light-off, temperature peak, starter off, idle. Watch three failures: hot start (temperature over the start limit), hung start (no acceleration to idle) and no light-off (wet start). On FADEC engines many airliners abort automatically on the ground, but you still watch.

Spool-up time

From flight idle a big turbofan needs around 5–8 seconds to reach go-around thrust. That is why approach idle exists, why a stabilised approach keeps the engines above idle, and why a go-around starts with the thrust levers first or together with the pitch-up, never after.

Temperature, altitude and thrust

Hot or high air is thin: fewer kilograms of air per second, less thrust or power. Jet engines are flat rated: they give full rated thrust up to a certain outside temperature, then the temperature limit takes over and thrust falls. Reduced take-off thrust saves EGT margin when the runway allows it.

Bleed air and anti-ice

Hot air taken from the compressor heats the inlet and the wings and runs the air conditioning. It is not free: thrust or torque drops and EGT or ITT rises. Performance charts tell you the penalty for take-off with anti-ice on.

Engine failure on a twin

Fly first: maintain control and speed (blue line on a piston twin, V2 or the OEI speed on a turbine). Then identify, verify and secure: on a turboprop or piston twin the propeller must be feathered; on a jet you shut off fuel and, if there is a fire, discharge the bottles.

Diesel and avgas, side by side

Diesel (AE300): one lever, FADEC, Jet A-1, no mixture, no carb heat, no magneto check; ECU test before take-off; the engine needs electrical power. Avgas: throttle, propeller and mixture; lean with altitude; carb heat in carburettor icing conditions (which exist up to about +30 °C in humid air); magneto check; watch CHT and EGT.

Both alternators online. Each engine drives its own alternator; either one alone can carry the normal load. The battery is only there for starting and as a reserve.

Other systems
Landing gear

Many light twins, including the DA42, use an electro-hydraulic system: an electric pump pressurises the gear actuators, and the gear is held up by hydraulic pressure and down by mechanical locks. Three greens means down and locked. If the pump or electrics fail, an emergency extension lets the gear fall by gravity and lock. Know your aircraft’s gear warning logic (power lever and flaps) and the speeds Vlo and Vle.

Ice protection

Light aircraft approved for known icing use either pneumatic boots on the leading edges, or a fluid system (TKS on the DA42) that weeps de-icing fluid through porous panels. Pitot heat is separate and should be on whenever you fly in visible moisture. Fluid systems have a limited endurance: the fluid tank sets how long you can stay in ice.

Pressurisation

Turboprops and jets bleed air (or use electric compressors) to keep the cabin at an altitude of about 6000–8000 ft while flying high. An outflow valve controls the cabin altitude. In a rapid decompression: oxygen masks on first, then an emergency descent. Time of useful consciousness at FL350 is about 30–60 seconds, and roughly half that after a rapid decompression.

Vacuum and pitot-static

Older aircraft drive the attitude and heading gyros with an engine-driven vacuum pump; failure gives a slow, quiet instrument failure. Glass cockpits use AHRS and air data computers instead. See the pitot-static and compass labs for how each instrument lies when something blocks.

Fuel types

Avgas 100LL (blue) for spark-ignition engines; Jet A-1 (clear to straw coloured) for turbines and for approved diesel engines like the AE300. Putting jet fuel in an avgas engine can destroy it within minutes; the reverse is also dangerous. Check the fuel type at every refuelling, and drain samples for water before flight.

Fire and smoke

Engine fire: on a piston twin, fuel selector OFF and the engine shut down per the checklist; on a turbine, the fire handle shuts off fuel, hydraulics and bleed and arms the bottles. Electrical smoke: identify and isolate, ventilate, and land as soon as possible. Smoke that does not clear means land immediately.

Thunderstorms and wind shear

A cumulonimbus contains almost every hazard in aviation at once: severe turbulence, icing, hail, lightning, microbursts and gust fronts. Watch one grow, mature and die, fly around a cell on the radar and see where the danger reaches, then fly an approach through a microburst.

The life of a CB
Around a cell
Microburst on final
Types and warnings

Mature stage (15–30 minutes). Rain and hail get so heavy that they drag air down with them: now there are violent updrafts and downdrafts side by side, the worst turbulence there is. The downdraft hits the ground and spreads out as a gust front and possibly a microburst. Lightning, hail (also falling from the anvil), heavy rain. This is when the first rain reaches the ground. Stay well clear.

How far is far enough? Common guidance is to keep at least 10 NM from a thunderstorm echo and 20 NM from a severe one or one that is growing fast, and to pass upwind rather than downwind. Hail can fall from the anvil well away from the core, and the anvil itself does not show on weather radar, which only sees precipitation. Turbulence extends outside the visible cloud, and the gust front often runs up to about 15 NM (sometimes more) ahead of the rain, so do not land or take off with a storm close to the aerodrome. Do not fly under the anvil, never try to fly through a gap between two severe cells that are less than about 40 NM apart, and do not try to out-climb a growing cell.

The trap is the first part: the headwind makes you fast and high, so you reduce power. Seconds later the downdraft and the tailwind take away far more energy than you removed. A microburst lasts minutes and its outflow can be over 40 kt. Signs: heavy rain shaft or virga under CB, a ring of dust, wind shear warnings, rapidly changing ATIS wind. On any unexpected speed loss near the ground: full power, go around, follow the wind shear escape procedure. Here you ended far below the glide path.

Types and warnings
Where wind shear comes from

Thunderstorms and showers (microbursts, gust fronts), fronts (especially fast cold fronts), a low-level inversion with a strong wind above it (often at night), terrain and buildings near the runway, and sea breeze fronts. The TAF, the METAR (WS RWY…) and ATC reports from other pilots are your warnings.

Recognise it on the approach

Airspeed changes of more than about 15 kt, unusual power needed to stay on the glide path, vertical speed deviations of 500 ft/min or more, pitch changes, and a big difference between the reported surface wind and the wind on your display.

Escape manoeuvre

Maximum power, go around, pitch for the best climb your aircraft allows (in airliners, up to the stick shaker), do not change configuration until the aircraft is climbing safely, and follow the flight path, not the airspeed. Report it to ATC so the next aircraft knows.

Ingredients

Three things: deep unstable air, plenty of moisture in the lower levels, and something to lift it (daytime heating, a cold front, hills, or converging air). With strong wind shear as well, storms become organised and long-lived.

Types

Air-mass storms: isolated, afternoon, over land in summer or over warm sea in winter. Frontal: in a line along a cold front, any time of day. Squall line: a long line ahead of a cold front, often the most violent. Orographic: over mountains. Embedded: hidden inside layer cloud of a warm front or occlusion, the most dangerous for IFR.

In METAR, TAF and SIGMET

CB after a cloud layer (SCT030CB), TS for thunderstorm, +TSRA, TSGR with hail, VCTS in the vicinity (8–16 km). SIGMET: OBSC TS (obscured by haze or darkness), EMBD TS (embedded in layer cloud), FRQ TS (frequent, little or no separation), SQL TS (squall line). An EMBD or FRQ SIGMET on your route is a reason to re-plan.

If you get caught

Fly attitude, not altitude: keep the wings level and the attitude steady, accept height changes, and fly the turbulence penetration speed (around manoeuvring speed). Do not turn back inside the cloud unless you are sure it is the shortest way out. Cockpit lights full bright against lightning, pitot heat and anti-ice on, seat belts tight, tell ATC.

Light aircraft

Without weather radar, stay visual and keep well clear; use datalink weather and lightning detection for planning, not for threading between cells, because the picture can be several minutes old. On the ground, a storm approaching the aerodrome, or within about 10–15 NM of it, means waiting: the gust front and wind shear arrive before the rain.

Related labs

Why the air rises in the first place is in Clouds, stability and fog. Pressure systems and the wind are in Pressure, fronts and wind. Icing and turbulence in general are in Icing and turbulence.

Air flows from high to low pressure, but the Earth turns underneath it. The Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the right in the northern hemisphere, so above the friction layer the wind ends up blowing along the isobars (the geostrophic wind): anticlockwise round a low, clockwise round a high. The closer the isobars, the stronger the wind. Near the ground friction slows it and turns it towards the low pressure, about 30° over land and 10° over the sea (dashed arrow). Buys Ballot: back to the wind, the low is on your left. Flying from high towards low pressure, an altimeter left on the old QNH reads too high: “high to low, look out below”.

Three forces. The pressure gradient force pushes air from high towards low pressure; the closer the isobars, the stronger it is. As soon as the air moves, the Coriolis effect (the Earth turning underneath) deflects it to the right in the northern hemisphere, more strongly the faster it moves and the higher the latitude. Above about 2000–3000 ft the two balance, and the wind blows along the isobars: the geostrophic wind. Near the ground friction slows the wind, Coriolis gets weaker, and the pressure force wins a little: the surface wind backs (turns anticlockwise) towards the low, about 30° over land and 10° over the sea, and drops to roughly half (land) or two-thirds (sea) of the wind aloft. So when you climb out, expect the wind to veer and increase.

Sea breeze. On a sunny day the land heats up much faster than the sea. Air rises over the land, and cooler sea air flows in underneath: an onshore wind of typically 10–15 kt, starting late morning, reaching 1000–2000 ft deep and up to 20–40 km inland, strongest in the afternoon. A runway that had a crosswind or tailwind in the morning can have a headwind in the afternoon, and the sea-breeze front can bring a line of cumulus and turbulence inland. At night the process reverses into a weaker land breeze.

Pressure and wind
Low pressure

Air converges near the ground and rises: cloud and rain. In the northern hemisphere the wind blows anticlockwise round a low. Fronts are tied to lows.

High pressure

Air sinks and warms: little cloud, light wind, clockwise round the high. In winter the sinking air can trap fog, low stratus and haze under an inversion for days.

Buys Ballot

Back to the wind in the northern hemisphere: the low is on your left. Flying towards a low you get drift to the right and the altimeter reads too high if you do not reset: high to low, look out below.

Isobars and wind speed

Close isobars mean strong wind. Near the ground friction slows the wind and turns it towards the low: about 30° over land and 10° over sea, at roughly half (land) to two-thirds (sea) of the gradient wind.

Air masses

Maritime polar air: cold, unstable, showers and good visibility. Tropical maritime: warm, moist, stable, low stratus and fog over cold sea. Continental air in winter: very cold and dry.

Reading the charts

On coloured surface analysis charts: red half-circles are warm fronts, blue triangles cold fronts, purple alternating occlusions. The symbols point the way the front moves.

Clouds, stability and fog

Almost all weather starts the same way: air is cooled until it reaches its dew point. Lift a parcel of air and see whether it keeps rising into a cumulus or a thunderstorm, or sinks back and spreads out as a flat layer. Then cool a clear, calm night and watch fog form.

Three lapse rates. Rising air that is not saturated cools at the dry adiabatic lapse rate, about 3 °C per 1000 ft. Once it reaches its dew point, cloud forms and condensation releases heat, so it cools more slowly, at the saturated rate of about 1.5 °C per 1000 ft in warm air (up to nearly 3 °C in very cold air). The air around has its own lapse rate (ISA: 2 °C per 1000 ft). The parcel keeps rising as long as it is warmer than the air around it. Here the air around cools faster than saturated air but slower than dry air: conditionally unstable. Dry air would sink back, but once the parcel is in cloud it is warmer than its surroundings and accelerates upwards. Heaped cloud, showers and turbulence; with deep instability and plenty of moisture, thunderstorms.

Radiation fog. A clear sky lets the ground lose heat, the air next to it cools to its dew point, and a light wind of about 2–7 kt mixes it through a few hundred feet. It is often thickest just after sunrise and usually clears as the sun heats the ground, from the edges inwards. Under an overcast sky or in winter with a weak sun it may last all day.

In the aircraft
Cloud base from the METAR

For convective cloud, (temperature − dew point) × 400 ft gives an estimate of the base above the ground. 25/13 gives about 4800 ft. It works poorly for layer cloud brought in by a front.

Advection fog

Warm, moist air moving over a colder surface: sea fog in spring and early summer along the coast, or mild air over snow in winter. It can form at any time of day, cover large areas, and persist in stronger wind than radiation fog (up to 15–20 kt).

Other fog

Frontal fog: rain from a warm front saturates the cold air below. Hill fog: stratus touching the high ground, often in orographic lift. Steam (arctic sea smoke): very cold air over open, warmer water.

Visibility terms

Mist (BR): 1000–5000 m with humid air. Fog (FG): below 1000 m. Haze (HZ): dry particles. Slant visibility on final can be much worse than the reported ground visibility, and RVR is measured along the runway.

Stability in the forecast

Look for cues: CU, TCU, CB and SH in the METAR and TAF mean unstable air; ST, SC, BR, FG and haze mean stable air. Stable means smooth but murky; unstable means bumpy, good visibility between showers, and icing in the tops.

Ways air is lifted

Heating from below (convection), hills and mountains (orographic), fronts (frontal), and air converging into a low (convergence). All of them end the same way: cooling to the dew point.

Mountain waves. They need wind of about 20–25 kt or more blowing roughly at right angles across a ridge, increasing with height, and a stable layer near the ridge top. The air then oscillates downwind like water behind a rock: smooth, strong up- and downdrafts that can exceed 2000 ft/min, lenticular clouds at the crests if there is moisture, and a rotor below the first crests at about ridge height, with severe turbulence. The lee side of the ridge has the strongest downdraft. Cross ridges at 45° so you can turn away, with at least 2000–3000 ft clearance, and expect the altimeter to over-read in the strong winds. A SIGMET SEV MTW warns of it.

Wake vortices sink and drift
Aircraft ahead
Light

Vortices sink several hundred feet per minute, typically to 500–1000 ft below the flight path, and from Heavy and Super aircraft more than 1000 ft. They drift with the wind. A light crosswind of about 1–5 kt can hold the upwind vortex over the touchdown zone, and a light quartering tailwind is the worst case: it can push the vortices forward onto the approach path and the touchdown zone. Stay above the path of the aircraft ahead and land beyond its touchdown point; take off before its rotation point, or wait.

Medium → Light	5 NM	2 min

ICAO categories from Doc 4444. Many European airports use RECAT-EU with other values; the AIP for each aerodrome decides.
Other hazards
Reporting turbulence

ICAO and SERA air-reports use two levels. Moderate: moderate changes in attitude or altitude, the aircraft stays in positive control, about 0.5–1.0 g at the centre of gravity. Severe: abrupt changes, the aircraft may be momentarily out of control, more than 1.0 g. (The FAA scale adds light and extreme.) Report moderate or severe turbulence to ATC: the next pilot needs it.

Ice on the ground

Frost, snow or ice on the wing must be removed before take-off: even a thin layer like sandpaper can raise the stall speed a lot and cut lift. After de-icing, the anti-icing fluid only protects for the holdover time, which depends on fluid type, temperature and precipitation. Check the wing again if you wait too long.

Mountain waves

Strong wind across a ridge in stable air: smooth lenticular clouds, strong up- and downdrafts downwind, rotor turbulence below the crests. Cross ridges with plenty of height (at least 2000–3000 ft above the ridge, more in strong wind) and at 45°, so you can turn away.

Clear air turbulence

Near jet streams and tropopause folds, with no cloud to warn you. Look at SIGWX charts and pilot reports; seat belts on.

Related labs

Thunderstorms, the worst of both icing and turbulence, have their own lab: Thunderstorms and CB. Microbursts and low-level wind shear are in Thunderstorms and wind shear, and fog in Clouds, stability and fog.

Volcanic ash and sand

Ash melts in turbine engines and sandblasts windows; it does not show on weather radar. Follow ash advisories and NOTAM. Dust and sand reduce visibility to near zero in minutes.

The altimeter shows altitude above mean sea level.

QNH

Shows altitude above mean sea level. On the ground it shows the aerodrome elevation. Used below the transition altitude, and the setting charts and terrain heights are built around.

QFE

Shows height above the aerodrome. On the runway it shows zero. Used by some operators and in some circuits, and with military traffic.

Shows pressure altitude, used for flight levels. Everyone uses the same setting, so aircraft stay separated from each other even though nobody shows their true altitude.

Climbing: set standard when passing the transition altitude. Descending: set QNH when passing the transition level. The layer in between is the transition layer, where you do not level off.

Wind and weather
Steady wind

The pitot tube measures air moving past the aircraft, not the ground. A steady head or tailwind changes the groundspeed, never the indicated airspeed.

Gusts and wind shear

A sudden change of wind changes the airflow before the aircraft has accelerated: a headwind gust gives a short increase in IAS, a loss of headwind a drop. That is why you add half the gust to the approach speed.

Icing

Visible moisture and temperatures near or below 0 °C can ice the pitot tip. Pitot heat ON before you enter cloud, and check the PITOT HEAT annunciation.

Heavy rain

Water can enter the tube. The drain hole lets it out; a blocked drain can give erratic or frozen readings.

On the ground

Insects nest in uncovered pitot tubes, and tape from washing is left on static ports. Pitot cover off and ports checked on every walk-around; airspeed alive early on the take-off roll.

Position error

At high angles of attack and with flaps the airflow at the ports is disturbed. That is why IAS differs from CAS; the correction table is in the flight manual.

Rules of thumb: on a 3° path you lose about 318 ft per NM, and the rate of descent is about groundspeed × 5 (more exactly × 5.3). Half the groundspeed × 10 gives the same answer.

Segments and minima
2D and 3D

A 3D approach has vertical guidance to a decision altitude (ILS, LPV, LNAV/VNAV). A 2D approach has lateral guidance only and a minimum descent altitude (LOC, LNAV, VOR, NDB), flown as a continuous descent (CDFA).

Type A and Type B

EASA classifies by minimum: Type A has a minimum of 250 ft or more, Type B below 250 ft (CAT I, II, III). It matters for planning minima and alternates.

At the minimum

At DA (or the derived decision altitude on a CDFA) you need the required visual references to continue: approach lights, threshold, touchdown zone and so on. If not: go around, straight away, on the published missed approach.

Stable approach

A common operator rule: stable by 1000 ft in IMC and 500 ft in VMC: on path, on speed, configured, normal rate of descent and power, checklist done. Not stable: go around.

Temperature and baro-VNAV

On a cold day the true altitude is lower than indicated. Baro-VNAV paths become shallower, so these approaches have a minimum temperature on the chart, and low altitudes may need cold-temperature corrections.

Briefing it

Before the approach, brief it in a fixed order so nothing is forgotten. The briefing page uses TSADMM: threats, setup, arrival, descent, minimums, missed approach.

What to remember
VOR

VHF, 108–117.95 MHz, line of sight. Gives radials: magnetic bearings from the station. Accuracy about ±5° for planning. Check the Morse ident before you use it.

NDB and ADF

LF/MF, 190–1750 kHz, follows the curve of the earth. Errors: night effect around dusk and dawn, coastal refraction, mountains, and thunderstorms (the needle points at the lightning).

DME

Measures slant range, not ground distance. Overhead the station at 6000 ft it shows about 1 NM. The error is small when you are more than about 1 NM away for every 1000 ft of height.

Intercepting

Turn to a heading 30–45° towards the course, wait for the needle to come alive, then lead the turn. Inbound on the RMI: the needle head moves away from the heading index, towards the inbound course on the card; you are on course when the head reaches it (relative bearing = intercept angle). Outbound, the tail moves towards the heading index.

Wind correction

Hold a heading into wind and keep the needle steady. On the RMI inbound with a crosswind, the needle sits on the downwind side of the heading index by the drift angle.

Reverse sensing

With the OBS set to the reciprocal of the way you fly, a CDI shows the course on the wrong side. Always set the OBS to the course you want to fly, and check TO/FROM.

Threats and checks
Jamming and spoofing

GNSS interference is common in parts of Europe, including Northern Norway and around the Baltic. Signs: loss of integrity, jumping positions, wrong time or groundspeed. Have a conventional plan (VOR, DME, ILS, radar vectors) and report it.

Database

The navigation database follows the AIRAC cycle of 28 days. An approach must come from a current database and must not be edited by the pilot. Check the waypoints and altitudes against the chart.

RAIM prediction

Before an RNP approach without SBAS, check that RAIM is predicted for the ETA (NOTAM, a prediction service or the receiver). Make sure that, if GNSS is lost, you can still fly an approach that does not use GNSS, at the destination or at the alternate.

Modes and scaling

The CDI sensitivity changes automatically: en route (about 2 NM full scale), terminal (1 NM) and approach (0.3 NM on final). Check the annunciation shows the approach mode before the FAF; if not, do not descend on the approach.

Leg types

TF: track between two fixes, the most common. DF: direct to a fix. CF: course to a fix. RF: constant-radius turn; the aircraft must be RF-capable and the crew trained (specific approval only within RNP AR). Holds and some legs end at an altitude rather than a fix.

Cold and baro-VNAV

Baro-VNAV is built on the altimeter. Below the minimum temperature on the chart the real path is too low: use LNAV minima, or LPV if available.

Spatial orientation

Your body was built for walking, not for flying in cloud. Here you can see what the aircraft really does next to what your inner ear tells you, and why you must trust the instruments.

The three senses

The three senses
≈ 80 %
Vision

The most reliable sense, as long as you can see a real horizon. In cloud, at night or over featureless terrain it is gone, and the instruments must replace it.

Inner ear
Vestibular system

The semicircular canals sense rotation, but only changes in rotation. The otoliths sense linear acceleration and gravity, but cannot tell the two apart.

Body
Proprioception, “seat of the pants”

Pressure on the seat and in the muscles. In a coordinated turn the force always points down through the seat, so it feels like level flight.

The leans

In cloud the aircraft rolls very slowly to the right, below about 2 °/s, so the inner ear does not notice. You spot the bank on the instruments and roll briskly back to wings level. That roll is felt, and now you feel banked to the left even though you are level. Pilots lean against it in their seat.

What to do. Believe the attitude indicator, keep the wings level on it and the false feeling fades within about 20 seconds.

Other illusions

The tag shows what the illusion makes you believe, and the text what you will tend to do. The cure is the same every time: cross-check the instruments and the glide path guidance.

Narrow runway
feels high

Looks long and thin, as if you were high. You tend to fly a low approach.

Wide runway
feels low

Looks short and wide, as if you were low. You tend to fly a high approach and land long.

Upsloping runway or terrain
feels high

The runway looks steeper, as if you were high. You tend to fly low.

Downsloping runway
feels low

Looks flatter, as if you were low. You tend to fly high.

Black hole, water or snow
feels high

No detail between you and the runway. Most pilots feel high and descend below the glide path.

Rain on the windscreen
feels high

Refraction can make you feel higher than you are, leading to a low approach.

Haze
feels high

The runway seems farther away, so you tend to descend early and fly low.

Bright runway lights
feels low

The runway seems closer, so you may fly a high approach.

False horizon
wrong horizon

Sloping cloud tops or rows of ground lights are taken for the horizon, and you bank or pitch to match them.

Autokinesis
false motion

A single light stared at in the dark seems to move after a few seconds. Keep your eyes moving.

Coriolis
tumbling

Moving your head in a sustained turn triggers a violent tumbling sensation. Keep your head still in turns in cloud.

Elevator illusion
false motion

An updraft feels like a pitch-up, and you may push the nose down. A downdraft does the opposite.
